entry.title: I’m sorry, but I thought Notre Dame was supposed to JOIN A CONFERENCE
entry.summary: It’s practically a battle cry across college football whenever anyone invokes the name of Notre Dame. The impending expansion of the college football […]
entry.content:
It’s practically a battle cry across college football whenever anyone invokes the name of Notre Dame.

JOIN A CONFERENCE

Outside of it being annoying and completely ignorant of Notre Dame’s history, and in some ways the history of college football, the phrase itself might be history as well.

The impending expansion of the college football playoff to 24 teams is making some major waves in the sport as the system is changing course. Once the new 24 team playoff is in place, there will be NO more conference championship games. So, essentially, conferences are just scheduling partners with group media rights.

That’s exactly as lame as it sounds.

In a 18 team or 20 team conference, who in the hell is the true conference champion without some wild tiebreakers or just the luck of the scheduling draw? And again… who really cares when there is a massive national playoff on tap?

There really is no point.

The Miami Hurricanes are quickly coming to this realization.

The Canes, like Florida State and Clemson, are feeling the squeeze of being members of the ACC — a “second tier” conference according to some. They’re looking for a way out, and that way out could be independence.

“If we have to go independent, I like our chances because we are a national brand. I wouldn’t like to do that because scheduling [other sports] is really tough. It’s great for football but what about track, volleyball and the golf team?”

There really is no way of knowing what moves these schools will eventually make (if any) but it’s becoming clearer and clearer, that being in a conference (top tier or not) isn’t anything close to what it used to be. The program who is best suited to move forward in this new era is seemingly the Notre Dame Fighting Irish — who have been independent since day one.

Join a conference. Why? What’s the point? What difference would any of it make as we get into 2027?

You’re right… pretty much none.

If the entire world of college football has come down to maximizing football revenue and the playoff, it makes little sense to tie oneself to a group of schools just get a conference Boy Scout Patch on the uniform.

Independence yesterday. Independence today. Independence forever for Notre Dame, and maybe a few other programs finally figure it out.

entry.title: Notre Dame Football Midseason Grades: Defense
entry.summary: It’s hard to imagine anything being good after Notre Dame’s loss to BYU. The loss looked and felt so devastating, that it’s easy and understandable to get lost in a sea of negativity. It would be easy to throw this team under the bus and dismiss anything good — and maybe it’s the most honest, […]
entry.content:
It’s hard to imagine anything being good after Notre Dame’s loss to BYU. The loss looked and felt so devastating, that it’s easy and understandable to get lost in a sea of negativity. It would be easy to throw this team under the bus and dismiss anything good — and maybe it’s the most honest, but I doubt it.

While 7 games is more than half of 12 (amazing math) we’re in the bye week, so let’s break out the midterm grades for the offense.

DEFENSIVE LINE A-

I don’t remember when Jason Onye went down against Wisconsin, but it was fairly early in the game. Against BYU Notre Dame was finally at full strength along the defensive line since that game, and that lasted for 5 plays before Traore was ejected. Still… this unit has been solid all season, and has been the main driver for havoc plays by the defense. The rotation is solid and we have been seeing more than a handful of players get their snaps in on the inside and outside of the lines while maintaining the same type of production.

LINEBACKERS B+

This is a tough grade. Notre Dame has the 3rd ranked rushing defense in the country, and they have only allowed 3 rushing touchdowns all season. And yet… they aren’t getting home with the blitz, and have been visibly out of position defending the pass (which looks like a true weakness/liability). I think they could easily be an A here, but the rotation seems off somehow. Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa needs to be on the field more.

DEFENSIVE BACKS B+

ANOTHER tough grade here for what was arguably the best defensive backfield in the country coming into the season, but… with the glory comes the responsibility. Notre Dame’s 3rd down defense is ranked 88th in the country, and right or wrong, so much of that is in the hands of the secondary.

Brauntae Johnson’s injury has been more costly than we originally thought. Adon Shuler has really struggled at times this season, and you have to think that if Johnson was healthy, the Talich/Johnson combo would be just fine.

Again, before you think this B+ grade for the first 7 games is too rough, Notre Dame’s pass efficiency defense is ranked 37th in the country. The potential to be so much better is obviously there, but their zone play hasn’t been good — and it was awful against BYU.

COACHING C

Chris Ash has all of us in a twist (and rightfully so) but I’m not seeing much of anything from Aaron Henry or Brian Jean-Mary that gives me much hope of improvement coming from their coaching. Charlie Partridge, however, seems to be a a real difference maker on the defensive line. Again — most of the problems we see on the defensive side of the ball looks like a Chris Ash issue against teams with a pulse. Despite having an incredible amount of talent, they look out of position and confused. How?!

OVERALL A-

So how in the hell can I give an overall grade of A- with the list of grades I just gave? Well, this isn’t school, and I am most definitely me. Notre Dame is ranked 1st in total defense and 5th in scoring defense. Of course I’m overreacting to the BYU game, but when it’s the biggest game to date and it looked the way it did — you kind of have to. Again, this defense is incredibly talented and will still be very capable of shutting its opponents down the rest of the season — yes even Miami.

entry.content:
In some of the most unsurprising news bits of the day… Notre Dame’s Hannah Hidalgo was named as a Preseason AP All-American.

Hidalgo Named AP Preseason All-American

SOUTH BEND, Ind. – Senior guard Hannah Hidalgo has been selected as a Preseason AP All-American, adding another honor to her decorated career.

Already named the Preseason ACC Player of the Year earlier this month, Hidalgo enters her senior season at Notre Dame as one of the nation’s premier players after putting together one of the most statistically dominant seasons in college basketball history a year ago. She led the ACC in scoring at 25.3 points per game and the nation in steals at 5.6 per game, while averaging 6.9 rebounds and 5.2 assists per contest. She is the only men’s or women’s college basketball player this century to average at least 25 points, five rebounds, five assists and five steals per game. Her 202 steals set an NCAA single-season record.

Hidalgo has also joined an exclusive group of four major-conference players this century to record at least 2,000 points, 500 rebounds, 400 assists and 400 steals in a career: Alana Beard (Duke), Shernise Johnson (Miami) and Armintie Price (Ole Miss). Hidalgo is the first to reach those milestones before completing her junior season.

Notre Dame opens the season with an exhibition against Truman State on Oct. 26 at 7 p.m. ET inside Purcell Pavilion before beginning the regular season against Villanova on Nov. 1 at noon ET at the Eternal City Tip-Off in Rome on FS1.

entry.title: Notre Dame Football Midseason Grades: Offense
entry.summary: It’s hard to imagine anything being good after Notre Dame’s loss to BYU. The loss looked and felt so devastating, that it’s easy and understandable to get lost in a sea of negativity. It would be easy to throw this team under the bus and dismiss anything good — and maybe it’s the most honest, […]
entry.content:
It’s hard to imagine anything being good after Notre Dame’s loss to BYU. The loss looked and felt so devastating, that it’s easy and understandable to get lost in a sea of negativity. It would be easy to throw this team under the bus and dismiss anything good — and maybe it’s the most honest, but I doubt it.

While 7 games is more than half of 12 (amazing math) we’re in the bye week, so let’s break out the midterm grades for the offense.

QUARTERBACK A-

This is, of course, a grade that reflects almost entirely the play of CJ Carr. I do want to say, however, the backups for the Irish have done a really great job when given the opportunity to get some snaps.

Carr gets an A-, but he is mostly an enigma to me right now. While he is among the nation’s leaders in passing touchdowns (1oth/16) he is is just 21st in the country in passing efficiency (which could be a little misleading as he has only thrown 1 interception this season).

Carr’s biggest question marks are his ability to take over a WIN a big game, and I still am not convinced that the constant checks and audibles are a good thing or even necessary half of the time.

He throws touchdowns and doesn’t throw interceptions. I’d like to see a little more of him using his legs, but he is clearly the driver of this offense which is scoring over 41 points a game.

OFFENSIVE LINE B+

This is a probably a little harsh for this unit. CJ Carr has only been sacked twice this season, and keeping him upright is priority one for this unit and this team. And yet… it took a few games for this line to come together.

It was a slow start for the Irish big boys, but once the personnel switch happened (Sullivan Absher for Styles Prescod) you could tell they should get better over the weeks — and they did. Will Black, for example, has gotten better over the course of the year, but he’s still a first year starter who has had his own moments of struggle. Anthonie Knapp has been good enough to earn All-American status, but my boy Ashton Craig… his snaps continue to be low, over and over again.

TIGHT ENDS C+

I’m very aware of the importance of Notre Dame’s tight ends when it comes to the running game, but their impact in the passing game is virtually nonexistent. The tight ends have a combined 20 receptions for 140 yards and 3 touchdowns. This is a far cry from the production Notre Dame is used to as “TEU” and that lack of production was on full display against BYU.

WIDE RECEIVERS B-

Only three Notre Dame wide receivers have double digit receptions through 7 games, and obviously that’s Jordan Faison, Micah Gilbert, and Jaden Greathouse. It’s been a really solid year for Faison and Gilbert so far, and Greathouse is starting to look more like 2024 playoff Jaden Greathouse. And yet… in non-garbage time, the Irish don’t rotate the way a high caliber offense should, and it shows throughout the course of the game. The group has been good, but they need more from someone outside of that leading trio.

RUNNING BACKS B

Notre Dame is just a little bit shy of averaging 5 yards per carry as a team, but Jonaz Walton is averaging 7.5 YPC by himself… but for whatever reason, he wasn’t trusted enough to get the bulk of the carries against BYU. That job went to Nolan James, and while he performed well, it’s hard not to imagine that if the carries were flipped with Walton — the freshman is breaking a few of those for big, big gains. The group gets a B, but should be more like an A if the load was managed differently.

COACHING C+

With maybe the exception of Joe Rudolph, the offensive staff just hasn’t produced a product yet that demands respect as a national championship contender. Whether it’s the lack of a real WR rotation, the slow roll of getting Jonaz Walton more carries, tight ends not being very Notre Dame like in the passing game, numerous 3rd downs when the pass catcher is in front of the sticks, too many CJ Carr checks — or just a lack of imagination overall, I can’t, in good faith, offer a better grade than this.

OVERALL B-

It may seem a bit harsh considering the offense is averaging over 40 points a game after 7 games, but Mike Denbrock has a real problem on his hands when facing top teams. The drive after intercepting Bear Bachmeier, or lack there of, is an indictment on whatever it is they are trying to do.

They have to get better if they have any hopes to playing in the college football playoff this season.

entry.title: The Wayward Train: My Dad’s Notre Dame Thanksgiving Adventure in 1963
entry.summary: An unforgettable Thanksgiving, a football game at Yankee Stadium, and a train ride that took an unexpected detour through Canada. Since Notre Dame has a bye week, I thought we’d take this week’s Throwback Thursday a little off the rails. Literally. Instead of revisiting a memorable victory or one of those classic Notre Dame football […]
entry.content:
An unforgettable Thanksgiving, a football game at Yankee Stadium, and a train ride that took an unexpected detour through Canada.

Since Notre Dame has a bye week, I thought we’d take this week’s Throwback Thursday a little off the rails.

Literally.

Instead of revisiting a memorable victory or one of those classic Notre Dame football games that still makes us smile, I’m sharing a story from my dad’s college days. It’s a story that involves Thanksgiving on Long Island, a football game at Yankee Stadium, one of the most difficult moments in American history, and a train ride home that turned into an international adventure.

Oh, and there’s a photograph of my dad sleeping upside down in his train seat.

Yes, you read that correctly.

But before we get to the train, we need to go back to Thanksgiving 1963.

A Thanksgiving Invitation

My dad was a student at Notre Dame when his classmate Mike Fiore invited him and a few friends to spend Thanksgiving with his family on Long Island. The plan was to enjoy the holiday with Mike’s family, explore a little of New York, and attend Notre Dame’s Thanksgiving Day football game against Syracuse at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx.

Mike was studying civil engineering at Notre Dame, following in the footsteps of his father, who was also a Notre Dame graduate. My dad remembers Mike’s father as a highly accomplished civil engineer who had worked on bridge projects.

The Fiore family welcomed the young men into their home for the Thanksgiving holiday, treating them to a wonderful dinner and giving them the opportunity to explore Long Island and New York City during their visit. They arrived Wednesday evening, attended the Notre Dame–Syracuse game at Yankee Stadium on Thanksgiving morning, and spent the rest of the holiday weekend enjoying time with friends before heading back to South Bend on Sunday.

For a group of college students, it sounded like a pretty terrific Thanksgiving getaway.

But the timing made this particular holiday unlike any other.

On November 22, 1963, just six days before Notre Dame and Syracuse would meet at Yankee Stadium, President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas.

When I asked my dad what he remembered about that Thanksgiving, he told me the country was still very much in shock.

It’s difficult to imagine what those days must have felt like for a group of young college students. They were away from campus, spending time with friends, and looking forward to a football game, but the entire nation was grieving.

And Notre Dame’s football team had experienced that historic week in a particularly unusual way.

A Football Season Overshadowed by History

In 2018, Notre Dame published a fascinating retrospective titled “Yankee Stadium, Circa 1963,” written by Matt Storin, who had served as the senior manager of the 1963 Fighting Irish football team.

Storin, a member of Notre Dame’s Class of 1964 who went on to a distinguished journalism career, offered a firsthand look at a difficult season and an unforgettable Thanksgiving week.

Notre Dame had been scheduled to face Iowa on November 23, the day after Kennedy’s assassination. According to Storin, the Irish had already arrived in Iowa City and settled into their hotel when the game was canceled. The team returned to South Bend on Sunday morning, only to turn around and travel to New York on Wednesday for its Thanksgiving matchup with Syracuse.

The Irish were struggling through a season in which victories had been hard to come by. Under interim head coach Hugh Devore, Notre Dame had won just two of its first eight games.

There was also uncertainty beyond the football field. Storin recalled the economic anxiety surrounding South Bend as Studebaker announced plans to end automobile production in the city.

Between the assassination, the struggling football program, and concerns about the local economy, it was a particularly difficult time for the Notre Dame community.

Yet the football season continued.

Storin remembered the team arriving in New York and checking into the Waldorf Astoria. The traveling squad numbered fewer than 40 players, and the players had little time to prepare once they reached the city.

The Thanksgiving Day game would kick off at 10:30 in the morning, an unusual start time by today’s standards, before a crowd of 56,672 at the original Yankee Stadium.

For Storin, walking through the third-base dugout and onto the famous playing field was an unforgettable experience.

For my dad and his friends, it was another chance to cheer on the Irish.

Unfortunately, the game itself would provide yet another frustrating chapter in Notre Dame’s 1963 season.

Notre Dame vs. Syracuse: A Familiar Ending

The 1963 Notre Dame Football Review described Yankee Stadium as an unusual setting for college football. The enormous grandstands towered above the players, casting long shadows across the field and blocking much of the late-November sunlight.

The Irish had experienced several heartbreaking losses that season, and the Syracuse game would follow a painfully familiar pattern.

Syracuse controlled much of the early action but repeatedly failed to capitalize on scoring opportunities. On one promising drive, Orange running back Jim Nance fumbled near the Notre Dame goal line, and Tom Longo recovered for the Irish.

Eventually, Syracuse broke through when Wally Mahle connected with Billy Hunter on a six-yard touchdown pass. Dick Arrington blocked the extra-point attempt, leaving Notre Dame trailing 6-0.

Late in the second quarter, the Irish finally found some offensive momentum.

Starting at their own 14-yard line, Notre Dame put together an impressive 86-yard scoring drive. Nick Rassas gained 20 yards around right end, Jim Kelly hauled in a 15-yard pass from Sandy Bonvechio, and Tommy MacDonald helped move the Irish deep into Syracuse territory.

Then Notre Dame reached into its bag of tricks.

Bonvechio pitched the ball to halfback Frank Budka, who threw a touchdown pass to MacDonald in the end zone. Ken Ivan added the extra point, giving Notre Dame a 7-6 lead with just one minute remaining in the first half.

For a team that had struggled so much throughout the season, perhaps this would finally be the afternoon when everything came together.

The Irish defense certainly did its part.

Bill Pfeiffer intercepted a Syracuse pass in the third quarter, and MacDonald added another interception to his impressive career total. Bob Lehmann and Ken Maglicic also helped thwart Syracuse scoring opportunities as the Irish clung to their narrow lead.

But the fourth quarter brought another heartbreaking finish.

With 3:28 remaining, Syracuse quarterback Rich King connected with Mike Koski for the go-ahead touchdown. A successful two-point conversion extended the Orange lead to 14-7.

Notre Dame couldn’t answer, and the Irish fell to Syracuse by seven points.

In his 2018 recollection, Storin described the loss as the fourth time that season Notre Dame had surrendered a game-deciding score late in the contest.

He also remembered an exchange with a Syracuse player after the game. The player sympathized with Notre Dame’s difficult afternoon, and Storin replied that it had been much like the rest of the season.

Sometimes, that’s just the way football goes.

One interesting detail from Storin’s account is that Notre Dame wore green jerseys that Thanksgiving Day. The Irish wouldn’t wear green again until the famous 1977 game against USC.

And although nobody knew it at the time, the 1963 season was about to become an important turning point in Notre Dame football history.

Just 18 days after the Syracuse game, Notre Dame announced that Northwestern head coach Ara Parseghian would take over the program.

The Irish would go from a 2-7 season in 1963 to a 9-1 record in 1964, narrowly missing a national championship.

But back on Thanksgiving weekend in 1963, none of that was known.

My dad and his friends had enjoyed a holiday with the Fiore family, watched Notre Dame lose another close football game, and were preparing to return to South Bend.

And that’s when their adventure really began.

All Aboard the Wayward Train

Notre Dame’s Blue Circle Honor Society had organized special trains to transport students between South Bend and New York City for the holiday weekend.

My dad and his friends weren’t officially part of that organized student trip. They had traveled east to visit Mike Fiore’s family and attend the game, but they were aboard one of the student trains for the return journey.

The trains departed New York’s Grand Central Station on Sunday afternoon, December 1, with what should have been a relatively straightforward trip back to Indiana.

The scheduled journey was approximately 16 hours.

It took 24.

A December 5, 1963 article in The Voice, Notre Dame’s student newspaper, detailed the remarkable journey under the headline “Wayward Trains Make International Trip.”

According to the newspaper, freight train derailments forced the trains to abandon their planned route. Instead of traveling directly toward South Bend, the students found themselves heading north through New York, crossing the Niagara River into Canada, traveling across Ontario, and eventually reentering the United States at Detroit.

From there, the trains continued south through Michigan, passing through Jackson before finally reaching South Bend.

Two countries, three states, multiple border crossings, and nine hours behind schedule.

Not exactly the most efficient route home.

And the detour was only part of the problem.

The trains experienced shortages of food, water, and heat. Crews had to be changed at the borders. The hours dragged on, and the passengers grew increasingly restless.

Fortunately, they hadn’t lost their sense of humor.

The newspaper reported that the students entertained themselves by cracking jokes about their predicament.

At one point in St. Thomas, Ontario, someone suggested that a local drugstore owner could make a fortune by opening his doors to the hungry travelers.

They were so desperate for something to eat that they joked they’d even eat his corn pads.

When the train stopped after moving only a short distance, another student announced that they’d apparently lost their priority to a handcart.

And when someone finally noticed the train was moving again, another passenger spotted an elderly woman walking along the platform and joked that she’d been racing the train since Buffalo—and was winning.

I have to admit, I appreciate the sense of humor.

Although I’m guessing that after 20 hours on a cold train with very little food, some of those jokes probably weren’t quite as funny as they had been earlier in the trip.

Sleeping Arrangements, Notre Dame Style

As the journey stretched on, the students began looking for creative places to sleep.

Some curled up in luggage racks. Others stretched out on the floors of the club cars, slept beneath dining-car tables, or pulled chairs together to create makeshift beds.

And then there was my dad.

Somewhere along that very long journey home, a photographer captured him attempting to sleep in what may be one of the most ridiculous positions I’ve ever seen.

His feet were propped up on the headrest of his train seat, while his head hung down toward the floor.

Upside down.

I have no idea how anyone could possibly find that comfortable, but apparently desperate times call for desperate measures.

The photograph appeared in the December 5 issue of The Voice, accompanied by a caption describing the unusual sleeping positions students had adopted during the 24-hour return trip.

More than 60 years later, that photograph is still good for a laugh.

And I have to say, there’s something pretty wonderful about discovering your dad in an old Notre Dame newspaper, even if he happens to be sleeping upside down.

The Great Jackson, Michigan Food Run

Of all the stories my dad remembers from that train ride, one of the most vivid involves food.

Or, more accurately, the lack of it.

By the time the trains reached Jackson, Michigan, the passengers were absolutely starving.

The newspaper reported that complaints about the lack of food had become constant. Arrangements were eventually made to have refreshments available in Jackson, with the New York Central Railroad paying for coffee and doughnuts.

But my dad remembers something else.

When they finally had the opportunity to buy food, the students practically cleaned out the store.

He recalls that they bought just about every bit of food they could find.

After spending so many unexpected hours aboard a train without enough to eat, I imagine even the most ordinary snacks must have looked pretty appealing.

And knowing a little something about college students and their appetites, I’m guessing the shelves didn’t stand much of a chance.

Eventually, the exhausted travelers arrived back in South Bend, nine hours later than expected.

The newspaper called their transportation the “Wayward Train,” which seems like an appropriate name for a train that somehow managed to take a detour through Canada on its way from New York to Indiana.

But despite the delays, discomfort, and hunger, the students had something they probably hadn’t expected when they boarded that Sunday afternoon.

A story they would remember for the rest of their lives.

More Than a Football Game

One of the things I found especially interesting while researching this story was an editorial published in that same December 5 issue of The Voice.

Titled “The Student Trip,” it reflected on the behavior of the approximately 1,500 Notre Dame students who had traveled to New York for the holiday weekend.

Apparently, there had been concerns about what might happen when that many college students descended upon New York City.

But the editorial praised their conduct and suggested that the experience demonstrated a growing sense of maturity and responsibility among Notre Dame students.

It was a nice reminder that even in 1963, students understood that they represented something larger than themselves when they traveled away from campus.

And while my dad wasn’t officially part of that organized excursion, he was certainly part of the larger Notre Dame experience that Thanksgiving weekend.

A classmate had welcomed him into his family home. He had shared Thanksgiving dinner with friends, attended a football game in one of America’s most famous stadiums, and experienced an unforgettable journey back to campus.

All while the country was still mourning the loss of President Kennedy.

Looking back, I find the contrast between those moments especially striking.

There was the sadness and uncertainty of a nation in shock. There was the disappointment of another difficult Notre Dame football season. And there was the ordinary joy of young people spending a holiday together, sharing meals, laughing at their misfortunes, and making memories that would stay with them for decades.

Storin’s account also reminds us that better days were just around the corner for Notre Dame football.

The players and fans who left Yankee Stadium disappointed that Thanksgiving couldn’t have known that Ara Parseghian was about to arrive in South Bend and change the direction of the program.

History has a way of looking very different when we know what happens next.

And sometimes the little stories surrounding the big moments are the ones that stay with us the longest.

When I started asking my dad about that Thanksgiving weekend, I knew there was a funny train story involved. I knew there was an old newspaper photograph of him sleeping upside down. But I hadn’t realized how many pieces of Notre Dame history were connected to those few days in November and December 1963.

That’s what makes revisiting these stories so special to me.

Not every Notre Dame memory involves a championship, a legendary coach, or a last-second touchdown. Sometimes it’s about the friendships formed along the way, the families who opened their homes, and the unexpected adventures that became part of the college experience.

I’m grateful that my dad is still here to share these memories with me, and I’m especially grateful that someone at The Voice had a camera handy during that train ride.

Because otherwise, I’m not entirely sure I would have believed the sleeping position.

Notre Dame may have lost to Syracuse that Thanksgiving, 14-7.

But my dad came home with a story that’s lasted more than 60 years.

And thanks to a wonderfully ridiculous photograph, I get to share it with all of you.

Go Irish!

Historical Sources

  • Matt Storin, “Yankee Stadium, Circa 1963,” Notre Dame Athletics, November 14, 2018.
  • “Wayward Trains Make International Trip” and “The Student Trip,” The Voice, December 5, 1963.
  • Bill Cragg, “Same Old Story,” 1963 Notre Dame Football Review.
  • Personal recollections of my father, Frank Kirner, a Notre Dame student in 1963.

entry.title: Why are Notre Dame fans so mad?
entry.summary: It’s not a trick question, and it’s not some kind of “gotcha” thing. I actually thought about this last week while attending the Stanford game, as I sat next to a miserable piece of crap in Section 3 Row 20 seat 15 as he constantly berated every player and coach during the first half of […]
entry.content:
It’s not a trick question, and it’s not some kind of “gotcha” thing. I actually thought about this last week while attending the Stanford game, as I sat next to a miserable piece of crap in Section 3 Row 20 seat 15 as he constantly berated every player and coach during the first half of a blowout — and didn’t return for the second half. Why are Notre Dame football fans so mad right now?

I’m not saying Notre Dame fans shouldn’t be mad. Of course many of you out there are mad as hell, and I’m one of them. Still… there are 5 games left in the regular season, and an enormous amount of opportunity in front of this Irish football team.

Still… I get it.

View Link

At 6-1 the Irish are ranked No. 4 in the AP Top 25, although they are likely to drop a spot or two after the bye week for no reason other than cheeseburger karma. Notre Dame is still sitting in a good spot, but… what the hell man?

I put up a poll, but I could have used about 15 more options. Frankly, I’m mad as hell about having to deal with a ridiculous loss in the season of “leave no doubt” and if we’re being honest — I think most of the things we say we’re pissed about all ends up flowing in that direction.

I’m not here to scold — or even validate your feelings. I just think we need to get this off of our chests while we’re in the middle of the bye week.

S0, here’s out final call here at OFD to talk about it all. Whatever is pissing you off — let it out. Don’t worry if you feel ridiculous, we took ridiculous to a whole new level on the latest podcast, so you’re in good company.

entry.title: Notre Dame wants a home cupcake to start the season
entry.summary: It was announced yesterday that Notre Dame will open its 2027 college football season at home against the Kent State Golden Flashes. Notre Dame and the rest of the college football world are gearing up for the expansion of the college football playoff from 12 teams to 24 teams. The Irish are playing 10 Power […]
entry.content:
It was announced yesterday that Notre Dame will open its 2027 college football season at home against the Kent State Golden Flashes.

Notre Dame and the rest of the college football world are gearing up for the expansion of the college football playoff from 12 teams to 24 teams. The Irish are playing 10 Power 4 opponents in 2027 to go along with two G6 opponents (Navy and Kent State).

Notre Dame and Kent State were originally scheduled to meet later in the season.

Notre Dame was originally scheduled to host Kent State on October 2, 2027, a date first announced in May. However, according to a contract amendment obtained from Kent State University through a state open records request, the game has been moved to August 28, 2027, and will be played at Notre Dame Stadium in South Bend, Ind.

The schedule change aligns with the NCAA’s June decision to adopt a uniform 14-week regular seasonbeginning in 2027. Under the new format, most FBS programs will be permitted to begin their seasons during what is currently known as Week Zero, the weekend before Labor Day weekend, which will become the sport’s standard Week 1.

In the Marcus Freeman era, Notre Dame has never opened the season at home, and in all but one game, it was a considerable Power 4 opponent.

  • 2022 @ Ohio State
  • 2023 VS Navy in Dublin, Ireland
  • 2024 @ Texas A&M
  • 2025 @ Miami
  • 2026 VS Wisconsin in Green Bay, Wisconsin

It’s hard to know the exact reason why Notre Dame opened the Ocober 2nd date up, but maybe that’s to fit BYU in the fold at that point in the season. No matter the reasons, Notre Dame is stepping in and making the changes it wants moving forward. Notre Dame hasn’t opened a season against a G6 opponent at home since Temple in 2017 — so maybe they just want a change.

I’d like new hardwood flooring, but I digress.

BYU was the first team truly that gave the Irish a challenge in 13 […]
entry.content:
Welp. There was definitely some room for doubt on Saturday night. The Notre Dame Fighting Irish lost a wild game on Saturday night to the BYU Cougars in what many considered a true litmus test for how the team actually is. BYU was the first team truly that gave the Irish a challenge in 13 calendar months. The loss stings for a lot of reasons, basically making a game against #1 Miami a must-win.

With a loss and how the Irish came out very flat in the first half with so many costly and uncharacteristic errors in play and in coaching, we head into the Cheeseburger Bye Week with many questions.

So, a game like that will lend itself to MANY emotions and reactions, and definitely some overreactions. Here are a few from Saturday night that I saw online, and how this edition might be more “reaction” than “over.”

ND @ BYU: Overreactions We Saw Online

Was Saturday’s defensive performance fire-able? I don’t think so just yet, but I totally understand the sentiment. The defense seemed lost in the first half. It’s not like the defense lacks talent, but you had Leonard Moore get fooled a few times, KVA and the linebackers struggled, and you saw missed tackles from Shuler and others. I’m not sure what happened entirely, but it did look like Chris Ash wasn’t truly prepared for the tricky plays and gamesmanship that BYU showed, especially in the first half.

That all segues well into the next “not so over” reaction. Shoutout to Jude for bringing this one back, as usually this is pretty true in football games. Unfortunately, this ended up being wrong for once because BYU’s trickeration and confusion of the defense eventually rattled Notre Dame and got the Irish down by two scores.

Calling CJ Carr average is certainly an interesting take. CJ Carr generally speaking reads defenses very well, stays poised, especially in the pocket, throws a beautiful ball most of the time, and he can manage games well. Now, we haven’t seen him against a Top 10 team in over one year. But, he also just did not look like he was comfortable all night. So many overthrows, plus the fumble spike. I personally think he is way better than average. This might sound like loser behavior, but he did drive the team down ~70 yards to get a chance to win the game on the “final” play. He’s definitely above average, but he did show weaknesses that need to be addressed. We hope that was a one-off flukey, uncharacteristic game for him.

I had thought this, too, especially in the first half, but I’m shouting out Pat Rick here. That performance and losing that game felt like the days of BK. Not showing up in a tough road environment and causing all of the haters to be correct. It did feel like we went back in time with a game like that.

entry.title: Three things we saw in Notre Dame’s loss to BYU
entry.summary: Notre Dame is now 6-1 and ranked No. 4 in the AP Top 25 after a weird, wild, and controversial loss to the BYU Cougars. Yes, I think the Irish got hosed out of one final play, but none of that matters now. We saw 59 minutes and 59 seconds of football, and there are […]
entry.content:
Notre Dame is now 6-1 and ranked No. 4 in the AP Top 25 after a weird, wild, and controversial loss to the BYU Cougars. Yes, I think the Irish got hosed out of one final play, but none of that matters now. We saw 59 minutes and 59 seconds of football, and there are some things we learned.

Boubacar Traore, Most Important Man

Last week Boomer called Boubacar Traore a renaissance man, and he was absolutely right. This week… we got five plays out of Traore before he was ejected for targeting Bear Bachmeier on a late hit. Despite Notre Dame’s depth at the position, the loss of Traore was massive for the Irish in the game —particularly in the first half when the defense was on its heels and needed better play up front to slow down what BYU was doing. The loss of Traore might very well be the essence of the full reason for Notre Dame’s loss.

The Lack of Offensive Rotation is Brutal

This second thing was supposed to be about Jonaz Walton and I went looking for snap counts. While the entire deal about Walton is valid and should be talked about after only getting 10 of the 81 snaps after rushing for 181 yards last week… the wide receiver situation might be the most heinous thing about the offense. On a night where Notre Dame’s receivers couldn’t get much separation from Cougar defenders, maybe they were gassed? The elevation was well over 5000 feet and Notre Dame only used 4 wide receivers all night. Jordan Faison, Micah Gilbert, and Jaden Greathouse were out there for almost every snap, and the fourth… well that was Mylan Graham with a whopping two snaps for the night.

Defensive Confusion is Still a Thing

For a good part of the first half, Notre Dame’s defense didn’t just play poorly — they looked confused. Presnap lineups and adjustments had several defenders running to the spot they were supposed to be, and BYU was snapping the ball before they got there. It looked very much like the Miami game last year, and some of that confusion led to slow and soft play. This, of course, is a Chris Ash problem and they made the proper adjustments at halftime to hold BYU to just 126 yards and 7 points in the final 29 minutes and 59 seconds of play. But… this is still a thing and will kill the Irish in a few weeks against Miami if it’s not fixed for a full 59 minutes and 59 seconds — or do we play 60 minute games now?
